Why Nothing Else Has Worked, And What Actually Does+

You were right to try what you tried. It was just aimed at the wrong thing.

Your GLP-1 works on the gut-brain axis. It turns down the signal running between your brain and your gut, and that is exactly why the food noise stopped. The catch is that the same signal is what tells your gut to keep moving. Turn it down and the entire conveyor belt slows: stomach, small intestine, colon.

Everything you are feeling sits downstream of that one quiet signal. Food sits in the stomach and ferments, which is the rotten-egg burp that clears a room. Transit that used to take a day now takes three or four, and your colon spends every one of those hours pulling water back out of stool, which is why it arrives like cement no matter how much water you drink. The water never reaches the stool. The colon strips it right back out.

Your gut's motor is idling, not broken. And every fix on your shelf either shoves the exit or parks more freight on a belt that already stopped.

What actually works runs in the other direction. Wake the signal with apigenin, the flavonoid concentrated in celery juice, which supports the gut-brain signaling and the natural wave-like rhythm your medication turned down. Keep water in the stool with low-viscosity soluble fiber, the kind that dissolves completely and cannot pile up. Neutralize the sulfur itself with chlorophyll complex, at the source, instead of covering the smell.

You could piece all three together yourself. Or take them in one gummy.

Stop forcing the exit. Restore the signal.

The Laxative Treadmill+

Almost every GLP-1 user lands in the same place eventually: daily MiraLAX as maintenance, magnesium citrate on the bad weeks. Nobody chose that. It is what is left after everything else stopped working.

Here is what it is doing. Osmotic laxatives pull water into the colon. Your signal went quiet upstream, so you are flooding the exit of a belt whose motor is off. It forces one evacuation, restores nothing, and day one of the next backup starts immediately. That is why months of taking it perfectly leave you exactly where you started, except now you need it to go at all. Forcing is not fixing.

There is a second reason worth knowing. A large 2023 cohort study published in the journal Neurology found that regular long-term laxative use was associated with meaningfully higher dementia risk, roughly 50 to 60 percent higher among regular users, and the strongest association was found for osmotic laxatives specifically. An association is not proof of cause, and this is not a reason to panic. But if you have been taking one every day as prevention, it is worth asking what it was actually preventing.

Motilli is not a laxative. It does not force anything.

120 Grams of Protein, Zero Grams of Fiber+

Eating high protein on a GLP-1 is correct. The medication kills your appetite, so you protect your muscle with chicken, eggs, shakes, Greek yogurt. A hundred grams a day, sometimes more. All of it slow to digest, and almost none of it fiber.

So everyone tells you to add fiber. Twenty-five to thirty-five grams a day. And the fiber makes it worse, which makes no sense until you know what kind of fiber they mean.

Bulk fiber works by absorbing water and swelling into mass. On a normal gut that mass stretches the wall and triggers movement. On a gut whose signal has gone quiet, nothing responds to the stretch. You just parked more freight on a stopped belt. That is the worse bloat, the gas, and the brick feeling an hour after the Metamucil. Bulk fiber also demands water in order to swell, so it competes for the water your stool needed on a transit that is already over-drying it. Bigger, drier, harder to pass.

The answer was never zero fiber, and it was never bulk fiber. It is the low-viscosity soluble kind. It dissolves fully, adds no bulk, forms a soft gel that holds moisture in the stool instead of letting a slow colon strip it out, and it feeds the bacteria that help govern your gut's rhythm. Fiber that works with a slowed gut instead of against it.

What to Expect, Week by Week+

Week 1: The sulfur burps start fading. Less pressure under the ribs after meals.

Week 2 to 3: The cement lifts and mornings get predictable. Movements come back on their own, not forced and not urgent. 91% of users report regular movements by week 2.

Week 4 to 6: The loop starts running in reverse. The belt moves, so less sits and ferments, so there is less gas and less pressure, so the belt moves better still. Injection day stops being something you plan around.

Day 90: Locked in. The slowdown took months to dig in, and 90 days is how long it takes to run the whole thing backwards. That is why this is a 90-day reset and not a bottle.

One more thing worth knowing: the gut-slowing side of a GLP-1 is heaviest in the early phase, and over time more of the appetite control comes from the brain. This is about getting through the hard season with your gut intact, while keeping everything the medication is doing for you.
